questions.prompt: What is the core mistake in the paradox of choice?
choices: Assuming a bigger menu always improves the decision experience
Believing that fewer options are always better in every case
Thinking comparison is unnecessary

explanation.gentle: Yes. More options are getting too much automatic credit.
explanation.direct: Correct. Abundance is being treated as improvement even when it is causing overload.
explanation.competitive: That is the trap. The giant list is posing as a gift.

questions.prompt: Why does this bias feel attractive at first?
choices: Because more options seem to promise freedom and a better fit
Because larger menus always reduce comparison work
Because fewer options never provide enough quality

explanation.gentle: Right. Bigger menus look like more freedom.
explanation.direct: Correct. Abundance suggests flexibility before its cost becomes obvious.
explanation.competitive: Exactly. Possibility flatters first and bills later.

questions.prompt: Which example best fits the paradox of choice?
choices: A buyer faces so many similar options that choosing and feeling satisfied both become harder
A buyer compares three strong options using clear criteria and chooses confidently
A team removes weak options before entering final comparison

explanation.gentle: Yes. The menu is creating more burden than benefit.
explanation.direct: Correct. Extra options are increasing comparison cost and weakening commitment.
explanation.competitive: That is it. The list is eating the chooser.

questions.prompt: What makes this bias dangerous after the choice is made?
choices: Unchosen options can stay mentally active and reduce satisfaction
It proves commitment is never possible
It means every broad menu should be avoided completely

explanation.gentle: Yes. The alternatives can keep whispering after the decision.
explanation.direct: Correct. A large menu can keep second-guessing alive even when the choice is good.
explanation.competitive: Right. The menu keeps regret on payroll.

questions.prompt: Why can more options weaken commitment?
choices: Because extra alternatives increase comparison work and keep more what-ifs alive
Because commitment only works when there is no freedom at all
Because good options are always hard to recognize

explanation.gentle: Right. More visible alternatives can keep the mind unsettled.
explanation.direct: Correct. The chooser pays for additional options both before and after commitment.
explanation.competitive: Exactly. The menu keeps exits lit in the back of the mind.

questions.prompt: What is the practical correction in this chapter?
choices: Set criteria early and narrow the field before comparison takes over
Look at every option equally until the choice feels exhausting
Assume the biggest menu contains the best answer

explanation.gentle: Yes. The fix is to narrow the field before overload builds.
explanation.direct: Correct. Better judgment uses criteria and elimination before abundance turns into friction.
explanation.competitive: Exactly. Cut the list before the list owns you.

questions.prompt: What does the paradox of choice confuse?
choices: A larger menu with a better decision experience
Criteria with regret
Simplicity with passivity

explanation.gentle: Right. More options are being treated as automatically better.
explanation.direct: Correct. Menu size is being confused with decision quality and satisfaction.
explanation.competitive: Yes. The bloated list is posing as wisdom.

questions.prompt: Why can extra options stop helping after a point?
choices: Because they may add more comparison burden than real decision value
Because all variety is harmful once choice begins
Because criteria become useless when menus expand

explanation.gentle: Yes. The added option may cost more attention than it gives back.
explanation.direct: Correct. Marginal options can impose cognitive drag greater than their contribution to fit.
explanation.competitive: Exactly. The next option can charge more than it pays.

questions.prompt: What is the deepest practical correction in this bias?
choices: Make added options justify their comparison cost instead of assuming they help automatically
Reduce every choice to a single option whenever possible
Treat regret as proof that the choice was wrong

explanation.gentle: Yes. The chapter asks you to make options earn their place.
explanation.direct: Correct. Better judgment compares the value of an option with the cost it adds to the decision process.
explanation.competitive: Right. Make new options pay rent or get out of the room.

questions.prompt: What is the chapter's threshold question?
choices: Is this extra option improving the decision, or only increasing comparison and doubt?
How impressive is the size of the menu?
Which option keeps the most possibilities open?

explanation.gentle: Yes. That question tests whether the new option is really helping.
explanation.direct: Correct. It separates meaningful decision value from pure comparison burden.
explanation.competitive: That is the cut. Is the option paying rent or just eating attention?
